references.text: In the preceding verse ([ref:Luk 12:25|Luke 12:25]), Jesus asks who can add a single cubit to their lifespan by worrying – this forms the basis for the argument in verse 26: If you cannot do even something so small (ἐλάχιστον), why worry about the rest?

The parallel passage in the Sermon on the Mount ([ref:Matt 6:27-28|Matthew 6:27-28]) contains the same argument: No one can add a single cubit to their lifespan by worrying, and Jesus then asks why they worry about clothing – the same logic moving from the smallest to the greater.

In [ref:Matt 6:34|Matthew 6:34], Jesus summarizes the exhortation against worry: "Do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself." This expands on the point that worrying about "the other things" (τῶν λοιπῶν) is unnecessary.

The introduction to the entire passage ([ref:Luk 12:22-23|Luke 12:22-23]) provides the context: Jesus tells his disciples not to worry about life, what they will eat, or about their body, what they will wear. Verse 26 serves as a logical conclusion to this argument.

In [ref:Luk 12:28|Luke 12:28], Jesus continues by pointing to God's care for the grass in the field – a further argument that worry is unnecessary, reinforcing the point in verse 26 that we cannot manage even the smallest things.

In [ref:Sal 39:6-7|Psalms 39:6-7], the psalmist reflects on human powerlessness and the transience of life: "You have made my days a handbreadth." This confirms that humans have no control over even the smallest matters concerning life.

[ref:Fil 4:6|Philippians 4:6] exhorts: "Do not worry about anything, but let your requests be made known to God in everything with thanksgiving." Paul here offers the positive alternative to the worry (μεριμνᾶτε) that Jesus warns against.

[ref:1 Pet 5:7|1 Peter 5:7] encourages believers to cast all their worries on God, for He cares for them. This is the New Testament answer to the worry Jesus mentions – instead of worrying about what we cannot control, we entrust everything to God.
